title: Alhamdulillah, thirty-three
hook: all praise to Allah, for what is given

segments.voice: Yesterday: tasbih, subhanallah, glory be to Allah, from a root for swimming. Your line was glory. Did something stop you, and did you say the one word? Day one hundred fifteen.

Back on day three, a long time ago now, you met a word Muslims say like a reflex. Someone asks how you are: alhamdulillah. You finish a meal: alhamdulillah. You sneeze: alhamdulillah. The car starts on a cold morning: alhamdulillah. You learned it then as thank-you. Today it comes back, not as a reflex, but as a count. Thirty-three times, after the prayer, right after the glory. It's one thing to say thanks once without thinking. It's another to sit and say it thirty-three times, and find you still have things left to say it for. Today: the praise.
screen: `BACK ON DAY THREE.` → `A REFLEX, THEN A COUNT.` → `STILL THINGS LEFT TO THANK FOR.`

segments.voice: Alhamdulillah means all praise is for Allah, and saying it is called tahmid, from the root h-m-d, praise. It's the same root as the name Muhammad, the much-praised, and Ahmad, and Hamid. It's also the first words of the Fatiha, after the bismillah: praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds. So every rak'ah of every prayer begins with it. Notice it isn't quite thank you. Thanks, shukr, is for something you received. Hamd is wider. It's praise for who God is, whether or not anything just happened to you. That's why Muslims say it when things go well and, often, when they don't. A hadith in Sahih Muslim puts the two side by side: how wonderful is the affair of the believer, for all of it is good. If something good happens, they're grateful, and that's good for them. If something hard happens, they're patient, and that's good for them too. The same collection has a short line about weight. Glory be to Allah, subhanallah, fills what's between the heavens and the earth. And alhamdulillah fills the scale. In the tradition's picture of judgment, where deeds are weighed, this one word fills the pan all by itself. And there's one about ordinary life. Another hadith in Muslim says God is pleased with the servant who eats a meal and praises Him for it, and drinks a drink and praises Him for it. That's it. No great deed. Just noticing the food, and saying the word. Thirty-three of those, after every prayer, and the day starts to feel full.
screen: `H-M-D — THE ROOT OF MUHAMMAD.` · `NOT JUST THANKS, BUT PRAISE.` · `GOOD OR HARD, ALL OF IT GOOD.` · `ALHAMDULILLAH FILLS THE SCALE.` · then, large: `A MEAL, A DRINK, AND THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thirty-three on your fingers, with a thing for each. Rest your right hand, palm up. On each joint, name one thing, silently: a person, a meal, a bed, a body that works, a morning. If you pray, say alhamdulillah after each one. If not, say thanks, or just name it. Some counts will come fast. Somewhere around twenty, it gets harder, and the things get smaller and truer. Keep going to thirty-three. The bell holds the time.
Tahmid. Saying alhamdulillah, all praise is for Allah, the word that fills the scale; thirty-three after the prayer. Today's word.
Your line: thanks, again. At your next meal and your next drink, say it before the first bite and after the last sip. Day one hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: After each prayer, many Muslims say alhamdulillah thirty-three times following thirty-three subhanallah, and through the day they say it after eating, drinking, sneezing, and when asked how they are.

myth: alhamdulillah is only said when something good happens
hamd is praise for who God is; Muslims often say it when things are hard, too.
the Fatiha begins with the same words
praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds, right after the bismillah.
a hadith says God is pleased when someone praises Him for a meal
for eating a meal and praising Him for it, and a drink too (Muslim).

fork.setup: something hard has happened to you today. according to the hadith of the believer's affair, where is the good in it?
options: there's none; only good things are good
fork.reveal: how wonderful the believer's affair: good brings gratitude, hardship brings patience, and both are good for them (Muslim).

original.note: Arabic: all praise is for Allah. tahmid (تَحْمِيد) is saying it.

trapdoor: what you thought: alhamdulillah means thank God.
what it means: all praise is for Allah: wider than thanks, praise for who God is, in good times and hard.
what a scholar hears: the distinction between hamd and shukr; Muslim 223 on filling the scale; Muslim 2999 on the believer's affair.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 2999 (how wonderful is the affair of the believer)

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory; please confirm.

In Muslim 223, 'subhanallah and alhamdulillah fill (or fill between) the heavens and the earth'; the script attributes filling the space to subhanallah and filling the scale to alhamdulillah, following the common reading. Please check.
Day 3 of the path taught alhamdulillah as 'thank-you as a reflex'; this day deliberately returns to it.
